title: Shrimp Hide Red Pigment. 2 Minutes of Heat Reveals It 🦐
description:
Why do shrimp turn pink when you cook them? Raw shrimp look blue-gray because a protein twists their red pigment, astaxanthin, and heat unravels that protein so the pink shows, the same pigment that colors salmon and flamingos.

topic: Why do shrimp turn pink when you cook them?
script:
Your shrimp was blue-gray two minutes ago.
Why is it pink now?
The pink was there the whole time.
Shrimp eat tiny algae
packed with a red pigment called astaxanthin.
But inside a living shrimp,
a protein grabs that pigment
and twists it out of shape.
And a twisted pigment looks blue-gray, not red.
Now add heat.
The protein unravels and lets go,
and the pigment snaps back to its true color.
Pink!
Lobsters and crabs do the exact same thing.
And that same pigment is why salmon are pink,
and it helps paint flamingos pink too.
They all get it from what they eat.
So the color wasn't made in the pan.
It was just hiding.
Be honest, did you think raw shrimp were pink?
key_facts: Shrimp get the red pigment astaxanthin from the algae (and tiny organisms) they eat
In a living shrimp, a protein (crustacyanin) binds and twists astaxanthin so it looks blue-gray
Heat denatures the protein, freeing astaxanthin, which shows its natural red-orange color
Lobsters and crabs change color the same way
Astaxanthin is what makes salmon flesh pink and helps color flamingos, all from their diet
